name: Classics of Christian formation
about: Julian of Norwich, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross, Brother Lawrence, Thomas à Kempis, Thérèse of Lisieux, de Caussade, Francis de Sales, The Cloud of Unknowing, Evelyn Underhill and others, in contemporary English, adapted from public-domain translations.

items.text: The house of my soul is narrow; enlarge it, so that you may come in. It is in ruins; repair it. There is that in it which must offend your eyes; I confess it and I know it. But who will cleanse it? Or to whom should I cry, but you?
items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.source: Confessions (modern English, from the translation by E. B. Pusey, 1838)

items.text: But what do I love when I love you? Not the beauty of bodies, nor the fair harmony of time, nor the brightness of the light, so pleasing to our eyes, … None of these do I love when I love my God; and yet I love a kind of light, and melody, and fragrance, and food, and embrace when I love my God: the light, melody, fragrance, food and embrace of my inner self, where there shines into my soul what space cannot contain, and there sounds what time does not carry away, … This is what I love when I love my God.
items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.source: Confessions (modern English, from the translation by E. B. Pusey, 1838)

items.text: When he had said this, she would not be satisfied, but pressed him further, with pleading and many tears, to see me and talk with me. He, a little annoyed at her persistence, said, "Go your way, and God bless you, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish." She took that answer (as she often mentioned in her conversations with me) as if it had sounded from heaven.
items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.source: Confessions (modern English, from the translation by E. B. Pusey, 1838)

items.text: For I wondered that others, who are subject to death, were alive, since he whom I loved, as if he would never die, was dead; and I wondered even more that I, who was a second self to him, could live while he was dead. Someone put it well when he called his friend "half of my soul"; for I felt that my soul and his were "one soul in two bodies". So my life was a horror to me, because I would not live as half.
items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.source: Confessions (modern English, from the translation by E. B. Pusey, 1838)

items.text: So I was speaking and weeping in the most bitter contrition of my heart, when suddenly I heard from a neighbouring house a voice, whether a boy's or a girl's I do not know, chanting and repeating again and again, "Take up and read; take up and read." … I seized it, opened it, and in silence read the passage on which my eyes first fell: … I would read no further, nor did I need to: for instantly, at the end of this sentence, it was as though a light of serenity had been poured into my heart, and all the darkness of doubt vanished away.
items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.source: Confessions (modern English, from the translation by E. B. Pusey, 1838)

items.text: For anyone loves you too little who loves anything along with you that he does not love for your sake. O love, you who always burn and never burn out! O charity, my God, kindle me.
items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.source: Confessions (modern English, from the translation by E. B. Pusey, 1838)

items.text: Outwardly, nothing more than what is happening to everyone else; inwardly, faith discovers and unfolds nothing less than God doing great things. O bread of angels! Heavenly manna! Pearl of the Gospel! Sacrament of the present moment! You give God under appearances as poor and lowly as the manger, the hay and the straw! … God reveals himself to the humble in little things; and the proud, looking only at the outside, do not find him even in great things.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: The present moment is always filled with infinite treasures: it contains more than you are able to receive. Faith is the measure of these blessings: you will receive in proportion to your faith. They are measured by love too: the more your heart loves, the more it desires, and the more it desires, the more it receives. The will of God is always before you like an unfathomable sea, which the heart cannot exhaust: only as far as the heart is expanded by faith, confidence and love can it receive from its fullness. All created things could not fill your heart, for its capacity is greater than anything that is not God.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: All you who are thirsty! Know that you do not have far to go to find the fountain of living water; it springs up right beside you in the present moment. So hurry to it. Why, with the source so near, do you wear yourselves out running after shallow streams, which only stir up your thirst and give you only a little to drink? The source alone can satisfy you; it never runs dry.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: We know perfectly only what we have learned by experience, through suffering and action. This is the school of the Holy Spirit, who speaks the words of life to the heart; and everything we say to others should come from this source. Whatever we read, whatever we see, becomes divine knowledge only through the fruitfulness, the power and the light that possessing this experience gives. Without this knowledge, all our learning is like unleavened dough, lacking the salt and seasoning of experience; the mind is full of crude, unfledged ideas; and we are like the dreamer who knows all the highways of the world but misses the path to his own home.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: Everything is the hand of God. Everything is earth, air and water to the soul. God's action is more universally present than the elements.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: Forgive me, divine Love, for I am writing about my own failings, and I have not yet learned what it is to abandon myself to your hand. I have not yet given myself up to the mould. I have walked through your divine studios and admired all your works, but I have not yet learned the self-abandonment I need to receive the marks of your brush. At last I have found you, my dear Master, my Teacher, my Father, my dear Love! I will be your disciple; I will learn in no other school but yours. I come back like the prodigal, hungry for your bread.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: Lord, can it not be said that your children sleep in your bosom all through the night of faith, while at your pleasure you fill their souls with an infinite number and infinite variety of experiences that are really only holy and mysterious reveries? In this dark night of the soul they are filled with real and dreadful terrors, with anguish and weariness, which on the glorious day you will change into true and solid joys.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: The more we seem to lose with God, the more we really gain; the more he takes away our natural help, the more he gives us of the supernatural. We loved him a little for his gifts, but now that these are no longer visible, we come to love him for himself. It is by seeming to withdraw these felt gifts and favours that he prepares us for himself, the greatest of all gifts.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: Fulfilling the duty of each moment adds no more than an imperceptible point, and yet it is through these apparent trifles that God works his wonders. At times we are given a glimpse of these wonders here below, but we will understand them only in the light of eternity. How full of wisdom and goodness the ways of God are! He has taken on all that is great, so completely raising and ennobling the work of his grace and action, and leaving to the soul only what is easy and simple to do with the help of grace, that there is no one who cannot reach great holiness by lovingly fulfilling obscure and humble duties.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: The divine action frees the soul from the petty, anxious schemes that human prudence finds so necessary. Such precautions suit Herod and the Pharisees: but the Magi have only to follow their star in peace; the Child has only to rest in his mother's arms; his enemies advance his cause more than they harm it; the more they try to thwart and crush it, the more peacefully and freely he advances.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: The broad, solid, firm rock on which the faithful soul stands, sheltered from tides and storms, is the order of the divine will, which is always present with us, veiled under crosses or the most ordinary duties. Behind these shadows God's hand is hidden, sustaining and upholding those who abandon themselves to him.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: A life of self-abandonment is marked by mystery; it is a life that receives extraordinary, miraculous gifts from God through commonplace, chance events and encounters, where nothing is visible to human eyes but the ordinary workings of people's minds and the natural course of the elements. So the simplest sermons, the most commonplace conversations, the least elevating books become, for these souls, through the will of God, sources of understanding and wisdom. That is why they carefully gather up the crumbs of wisdom that the worldly-wise trample underfoot.
items.author: Jean-Pierre de Caussade
items.source: Abandonment (modern English, from the translation by Ella McMahon, 1887)

items.text: Daughter, if you wear a coat of mail or a hair shirt, fast on bread and water, and say a thousand Our Fathers every day, you will not please me as well as you do when you are silent and let me speak in your soul.
items.author: Margery Kempe
items.source: A Short Treatise of Contemplation, from the Book of Margery Kempe, in The Cell of Self-Knowledge (1521; ed. Edmund G. Gardner, 1910, in modern English)

items.text: Daughter, in nothing you do or say can you please God better than by believing that he loves you. For if it were possible for me to weep with you, I would weep with you for the compassion I have for you.
items.author: Margery Kempe
items.source: A Short Treatise of Contemplation, from the Book of Margery Kempe, in The Cell of Self-Knowledge (1521; ed. Edmund G. Gardner, 1910, in modern English)

items.text: For when a soul offers itself to Jesu truly and humbly, putting all its trust and desire in him, and diligently keeps him in mind, our Lord Jesu, when he wills, purifies the soul's affection, fills it and feeds it with the sweetness of himself, and makes his name, in the soul's feeling, like honey, and like song, and like anything delightful; so that the soul delights evermore to cry, Jesu, Jesu.
items.author: Walter Hilton
items.source: Of the Song of Angels, in The Cell of Self-Knowledge (1521; ed. Edmund G. Gardner, 1910, in modern English)

items.text: Chaste love is when you ask of God neither release from pain, nor increase of reward, nor even sweetness in his love in this life; … but you ask of God nothing but himself, and you neither care nor look to see whether you will be in pain or in bliss, so long as you have him whom you love. This is chaste love; this is perfect love.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Epistle of Prayer, in The Cell of Self-Knowledge (1521; ed. Edmund G. Gardner, 1910, in modern English)

items.text: For silence is not God, nor is speaking God; fasting is not God, nor is eating God; solitude is not God, nor is company God; nor is any other such pair of opposites. He is hidden between them, and cannot be found by any work of your soul, but only by the love of your heart. He cannot be known by reason, he cannot be gained by thought, nor grasped by understanding; but he can be loved and chosen by the true, loving will of your heart.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Epistle of Discretion in Stirrings of the Soul, in The Cell of Self-Knowledge (1521; ed. Edmund G. Gardner, 1910, in modern English)

items.text: Meditation on the four last things will be useful to you as long as you always end with an act of confidence in God. Never picture death or hell on one side unless the Cross is on the other, so that when your fears have been stirred by the one, you may turn with confidence to the other for help.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: In the royal galley of divine love there are no galley slaves; all the oarsmen are volunteers.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: Always be as gentle as you can, and remember that more flies are caught with a spoonful of honey than with a hundred barrels of vinegar. If we must err in one direction or the other, let it be towards gentleness. No sauce was ever spoilt by too much sugar. … To tell our neighbour wholesome truths tenderly is to throw red roses rather than red-hot coals in his face.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: Do not sow wishes in other people's gardens; do not want to be what you are not, but try most earnestly to be the best of what you are. Try with all your might to perfect yourself in the state in which God has placed you, and bear bravely whatever crosses, heavy or light, may be laid on your shoulders.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: When we remain unmoved in prayer and meditation, it comes not from any fault of ours but from the providence of God, who wants us to travel by land, and often by desert land, rather than by water, and who wills to accustom us to labour and hardship in our spiritual life.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: Be fair: neither accuse nor excuse your poor soul except after careful thought, in case, by excusing yourself when you should not, you become careless, and by accusing yourself without cause, you lose heart and become cowardly. Walk simply and you will walk securely.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: The sovereign Spirit of our God is everywhere, and without his will or permission no other spirit dares to stir. Those who fear this divine Spirit need fear no other. You are beneath his wings, like a little chick under its mother's; what are you afraid of? … I have now grown so strong in this confidence that darkness and the solitude of the night delight me, since in solitude I realise more fully the all-embracing presence of God.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: Who has told us that we are blameless? Perhaps these people see our faults better than we see them ourselves, and better than those who love us do. When truths displease us, we often call them slanders.
items.author: Francis de Sales
items.source: The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales, recorded by Jean-Pierre Camus (modern English, from the translation by J. S., 1910)

items.text: I saw that he is everything to us that is good and comforting for us. He is our clothing, who out of love wraps us, holds us close and encloses us all round in tender love, so that he may never leave us; being to us everything that is good, as I understand it.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: Also in this he showed me a little thing, the size of a hazelnut, in the palm of my hand; and it was as round as a ball. I looked at it with the eye of my understanding and thought: What can this be? And the answer came in general terms: It is all that is made. I marvelled at how it could last, for I thought that, being so little, it might suddenly have fallen into nothing. And I was answered in my understanding: It lasts, and always will, because God loves it. And so everything has its being through the love of God.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: Our Lord God also showed that it is a very great pleasure to him when a helpless soul comes to him simply, plainly and intimately. For this is the natural yearning of the soul, through the touch of the Holy Spirit (as I understand it in this showing): God, of your goodness, give me yourself; for you are enough for me, and I can ask for nothing less that would be full worship of you. And if I ask for anything less, I am always in want; only in you do I have everything.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: For our soul is so specially loved by him who is highest that it surpasses the knowledge of all creatures: that is to say, no creature that is made can fully know how much, how sweetly and how tenderly our Maker loves us. And so, with grace and his help, we can stand in spiritual beholding, in everlasting wonder at this high, surpassing, immeasurable love that Almighty God has for us in his goodness.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: For our natural will is to have God, and God's good will is to have us; and we can never stop willing or longing until we have him in fullness of joy: and then we can desire nothing more.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: For truly, as I see it, it is the greatest joy there can be that he who is highest and mightiest, noblest and worthiest, is also lowest and meekest, most intimate and most courteous: and truly this marvellous joy will be shown to us all when we see him.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: But Jesus, who in this vision told me all that I needed, answered with this word and said: It was necessary that there should be sin; but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: And then I saw that every kind act of compassion that a person has for their fellow Christians, out of charity, is Christ in them.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: I understood that we are now, as our Lord sees it, on his Cross with him in his pains and his Passion, dying; and if we willingly stay on that same Cross, with his help and his grace, to the very end, suddenly he will change his look towards us, and we will be with him in heaven. Between the one and the other there will be no time, and then everything will be brought to joy.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: Then our good Lord Jesus Christ said: Are you well pleased that I suffered for you? I said: Yes, good Lord, thank you; yes, good Lord, blessed may you be. Then Jesus, our kind Lord, said: If you are pleased, I am pleased. It is a joy, a bliss, an endless satisfaction to me that I ever suffered the Passion for you; and if I could suffer more, I would suffer more.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: A glad giver pays little attention to the thing he gives; all his desire and all his intention is to please and comfort the one he gives it to. And if the receiver takes the gift with high regard and gratitude, then the courteous giver counts all his cost and all his labour as nothing, for the joy and delight of having pleased and comforted the one he loves.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: Then we hope that God has forgiven us our sins, and it is true. And then our courteous Lord shows himself to the soul, merrily and with a glad face, with a friendly welcome, as if it had been in pain and in prison, saying sweetly: My darling, I am glad you have come to me. In all your woe I have always been with you; and now you see my love, and we are made one in bliss.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: So he says this: Pray inwardly, even though it seems to you to have no savour: for it is profitable, though you feel nothing, though you see nothing; yes, even though you think you cannot. For in dryness and in barrenness, in sickness and in weakness, then your prayer is most pleasing to me, though it seems to you to have little or no savour. And so is all your believing prayer in my sight.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: And thanksgiving also belongs to prayer. Thanksgiving is a true inward knowing, turning ourselves with great reverence and loving awe, with all our strength, to the work our good Lord stirs us to, rejoicing and giving thanks inwardly. And sometimes, out of sheer abundance, it breaks out into speech and says: Good Lord, thank you! Blessed may you be!
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: But sometimes it comes to our mind that we have prayed for a long time, and yet it seems to us that we have not received what we asked for. But we should not be downcast about this. For I am sure, from what our Lord has shown, that either we are waiting for a better time, or more grace, or a better gift.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: But often, when our falling and our wretchedness are shown to us, we are so frightened and so deeply ashamed of ourselves that we hardly know where to turn. But then our courteous Mother does not want us to run away, for nothing would displease him more. He wants us then to behave like a child: for when it is hurt or frightened, it runs quickly to its mother for help, with all its might.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: For we need to fall, and we need to see it. For if we never fell, we would not know how weak and how wretched we are of ourselves, nor would we fully know the marvellous love of our Maker. For in heaven we will truly see, without end, that we have sinned grievously in this life; and despite this, we will see that we were never hurt in his love, and were never of less worth in his sight.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: And these words, You shall not be overcome, were said very clearly and very powerfully, for assurance and comfort against all the troubles that may come. He did not say: You shall not be storm-tossed, … but he said: You shall not be overcome. God wants us to pay attention to these words, and always to be strong in sure trust, in good times and in bad.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: And from the time this was shown, I often wanted to learn what our Lord meant. And fifteen years and more afterwards, I was answered in spiritual understanding, in these words: Would you learn your Lord's meaning in this thing? Learn it well: Love was his meaning. Who showed it to you? Love. What did he show you? Love. Why did he show it to you? For love.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: And I saw most surely that before God made us he loved us; and this love has never slackened, nor ever will. And in this love he has done all his works; and in this love he has made all things work for our good; and in this love our life is everlasting. In our making we had a beginning; but the love in which he made us was in him without beginning: and in that love we have our beginning.
items.author: Julian of Norwich
items.source: Revelations of Divine Love (modern English, from the translation by Grace Warrack, 1901)

items.text: For truly, it is not lofty words that make a man holy and upright; it is a good life that makes a man dear to God. I would rather feel contrition than know how to define it.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: The one to whom all things are one, who brings all things to one, who sees all things in one, is able to remain steadfast in spirit and at rest in God. O God, who are the Truth, make me one with you in everlasting love. I often grow weary of reading and hearing many things; in you is all that I wish for and desire. Let all the teachers be silent; let all creation keep silence before you: speak to me, you alone.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: Surely, on the Day of Judgement we will be asked not what we have read but what we have done; not how well we have spoken but how holily we have lived.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: As fire tests iron, so temptation tests the upright man. Often we do not know what strength we have; but temptation shows us what we are.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: But God has now ordained it so, that we may learn to bear one another's burdens; because no one is without fault, no one without a burden, no one self-sufficient, no one wise enough alone; but we need to bear with one another, to comfort one another, to help, instruct and admonish one another.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: Shut your door behind you, and call to yourself Jesus, your beloved. Stay with him in your room, for you will not find such great peace anywhere else.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: Very soon there will be an end of you here; so think carefully how it will be with you in another world. Today a man is here, and tomorrow he is seen no more. … If you are not ready today, how will you be ready tomorrow? Tomorrow is an uncertain day; and how do you know that you will have a tomorrow?
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: A certain man, anxious in mind and constantly tossed between hope and fear, was one day overwhelmed with grief. He threw himself down in prayer before the altar in a church and, meditating within himself, said, "Oh, if only I knew that I would persevere!" And at once he heard within him a voice from God: "And if you did know it, what would you do? Do now what you would do then, and you will be quite secure."
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: Whoever knows how to walk from within, and to set little value on outward things, needs no special places and waits for no special seasons to hold communion with God. The inward man quickly gathers himself, because he is never wholly given up to outward things. No outward labour and no necessary work stands in his way; as events happen, he adapts himself to them.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: First keep yourself at peace, and then you will be able to make peace for others. A peaceable man does more good than a very learned one. A passionate man turns even good into evil and readily believes evil; a good, peaceable man turns all things to good.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: When Jesus is present, all is well and nothing seems hard; but when Jesus is not present, everything is hard. When Jesus does not speak within, our comfort is worth nothing; but if Jesus speaks just a single word, the comfort we feel is great.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: In these things you are not to be downcast or to despair, but to rest with a calm mind on the will of God, and to bear everything that comes upon you to the praise of Jesus Christ; for after winter comes summer, after night day returns, after the storm a great calm.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: No one understands the Passion of Christ in his heart so well as someone who has had some share of the same suffering himself. So the Cross is always ready, and waits for you everywhere. You cannot escape it wherever you run, for wherever you go, you take yourself with you, and will always find yourself.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: Blessed is the soul that hears the Lord speaking within it, and receives the word of consolation from his mouth. Blessed are the ears that catch the echoes of God's soft whisper, and do not turn aside to the whisperings of this world. … Blessed are those who long to have leisure for God, and free themselves from every hindrance of the world.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: Love is a great thing, a good above all others, which alone makes every heavy burden light and evens out every inequality. For it carries the burden and makes it no burden; it makes every bitter thing sweet and pleasant to taste. … Nothing is sweeter than love, nothing stronger, nothing higher, nothing broader, nothing more pleasant, nothing fuller or better in heaven or on earth; for love was born of God and cannot rest except in God, above all created things.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: Strive, my son, to do another's will rather than your own. Always choose to have less rather than more. Always seek the lowest place, and to be subject to all. Always wish and pray that the will of God may be fulfilled in you. See, a man like this enters into the inheritance of peace and quietness.
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.source: The Imitation of Christ (modern English, from the translation by William Benham, 1909)

items.text: In winter, seeing a tree stripped of its leaves, and considering that in a little while the leaves would be renewed, and after that the flowers and fruit would appear, I received a high view of the providence and power of God, which has never since been erased from my soul.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: I have always been governed by love, without selfish aims; and having resolved to make the love of God the end of all my actions, I have found reason to be well satisfied with my method. I am pleased when I can pick up a straw from the ground for the love of God, seeking him only, and nothing else, not even his gifts.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: For a long time I was troubled in mind by a certain belief that I would be damned; all the people in the world could not have persuaded me otherwise; but I reasoned with myself about it like this: I entered religious life only for the love of God, and I have tried to act only for him; whatever becomes of me, whether I am lost or saved, I will always go on acting purely for the love of God.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: We ought to act with God in the greatest simplicity, speaking to him frankly and plainly, and asking his help in our affairs just as they happen. God has never failed to give it, as I have often experienced.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: No art or science is needed for going to God, only a heart resolutely determined to apply itself to nothing but him, or for his sake, and to love him only.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: We ought not to grow weary of doing little things for the love of God, who looks not at the greatness of the work but at the love with which it is done. We should not be surprised if, in the beginning, we often fail in our efforts; but in the end we will gain a habit that will naturally produce its acts in us, without any effort on our part, and to our very great delight.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: He was never hasty nor dawdling, but did each thing in its season, with an even, unbroken composure and tranquillity of spirit. "The time of work," he said, "is no different for me from the time of prayer; and in the noise and clatter of my kitchen, while several people are calling for different things at the same time, I possess God in as great tranquillity as if I were on my knees before the blessed sacrament."
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: When I thought of nothing but ending my days in these troubles (which did not at all lessen my trust in God, and served only to increase my faith), I found myself suddenly changed; and my soul, which until then had been in turmoil, felt a deep inward peace, as if it had come to its centre and place of rest.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: As for my set times of prayer, they are simply a continuation of the same practice. Sometimes I think of myself there as a stone before a sculptor, who is to make a statue from it; presenting myself like this before God, I ask him to form his perfect image in my soul and make me entirely like himself.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: A little lifting up of the heart is enough. A brief remembrance of God, one act of inward worship, even on the march with sword in hand, are prayers which, however short, are still very acceptable to God; and far from lessening a soldier's courage in moments of danger, they do most to strengthen it.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: Lift up your heart to him, sometimes even at your meals and when you are in company: the least little remembrance will always be acceptable to him. You need not cry out loudly; he is nearer to us than we realise. … We do not need to be always at church to be with God: we can make an oratory of our heart, where we withdraw from time to time to talk with him in meekness, humility and love.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: I do not advise you to use many words in prayer: many words and long speeches are often the occasion of wandering. Hold yourself in prayer before God like a mute or paralysed beggar at a rich man's gate. Make it your business to keep your mind in the presence of the Lord.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: She seems to me full of good will, but she wants to go faster than grace. No one becomes holy all at once. I commend her to you: we ought to help one another by our advice, and even more by our good example.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: He is always near you and with you: do not leave him alone. You would think it rude to leave alone a friend who had come to visit you: so why should God be neglected?
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: I must soon go to God. What comforts me in this life is that I now see him by faith; and I see him in such a way that I might sometimes say, I no longer believe, but I see. I feel what faith teaches us, and in that assurance and that practice of faith I will live and die with him.
items.author: Brother Lawrence
items.source: The Practice of the Presence of God (Fleming H. Revell, c. 1895, in modern English)

items.text: And if he perseveres, I trust in the mercy of God for him, since no one ever took God as a friend without being richly rewarded; for mental prayer, in my view, is nothing other than being on terms of friendship with God, often talking alone with him who, we know, loves us.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: Oh, what a good friend you are, my Lord! How you comfort and endure, and wait for them to become like you, and meanwhile are so patient with the state they are in! You take into account the times when they seek you, and for a moment of repentance you forget their offences against you.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: I can speak of what I know by experience; and so I say, whoever has once begun to pray should never give it up, however wicked his life may be; for prayer is the way to amend it, and without prayer that amendment will be much more difficult.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: This was my way of praying: since I could not reason things through with my understanding, I tried to picture Christ within me; and I used to find it helped me to think of those moments in his life when he was most alone. It seemed to me that his being alone and afflicted, like someone in trouble, must allow me to come close to him.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: It also helped me to look at fields, water and flowers. In them I saw traces of the Creator — I mean that the sight of these things was like a book to me; it roused me, made me recollected, and reminded me of my ingratitude and my sins.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: He must rejoice and take comfort, and count it the greatest favour to work in the garden of so great an Emperor; … let him help the Lord carry the Cross, and think how he carried it all his life long; let him not look for his kingdom here, nor ever give up his prayer; and so let him resolve, even if this dryness should last his whole life long, never to let Christ fall beneath the Cross.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: This comparison pleases me; for very often, when I was beginning — and may our Lord grant that I have really begun to serve His Majesty — I mean begun in relation to what I have to say about my life — it was a great joy to me to think of my soul as a garden, and of our Lord walking in it. I used to beg him to increase the fragrance of the little flowers of virtue, which seemed to be beginning to bud, and to preserve them, so that they might be for his glory; for I wanted nothing for myself. I asked him to cut the ones he liked, because I already knew they would grow all the better.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: The soul may also place itself in the presence of Christ, and grow used to making many acts of love directed to his sacred humanity, and remain in his presence continually, speaking to him, praying to him in its needs, and complaining to him of its troubles; being glad with him in its joys, and yet not forgetting him because of its joys. All this it can do without set prayers, using instead words that suit its desires and its needs.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: His Majesty seeks and loves courageous souls; but they must be humble in their ways and have no confidence in themselves. I have never seen one of these lag behind on the road; and never a cowardly soul, even with the help of humility, make as much progress in many years as the courageous make in a few. I am astonished at the great things done on this road by encouraging ourselves to undertake great things, even if we do not yet have the strength for them; the soul takes flight and rises high, though, like a little bird whose wings are weak, it grows tired and rests.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: What the soul has to do in those times when it is raised to the prayer of quiet is nothing more than to be gentle and make no noise. By noise I mean the understanding going about in search of words and reflections with which to thank God for this grace, and piling up its sins and imperfections to show that it does not deserve it.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: With so good a Friend and Captain always present, who was himself the first to suffer, everything can be borne. He helps, he strengthens, he never fails; he is the true Friend.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: The pain was so great that it made me moan; and yet the sweetness of this excessive pain was so surpassing that I could not wish to be rid of it. The soul is now satisfied with nothing less than God. The pain is not bodily but spiritual, though the body has its share in it, even a large one. It is so sweet a caressing of love that now takes place between the soul and God that I pray God in his goodness to let anyone who thinks I am lying experience it.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: I was at prayer, and saw myself alone on a wide plain. All around me stood a great crowd of all kinds of people, hemming me in on every side; they all seemed to have weapons of war in their hands, to hurt me … In this distress of mind, not knowing what to do, I lifted my eyes to heaven and saw Christ — not in heaven, but high above me in the air — holding out his hand to me and protecting me there, so that I was no longer afraid of all that crowd, nor could they, though they wanted to, do me any harm.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: The vision left me in great tenderness, joy and humility. It seemed to me, though I did not know how, that our Lord was now giving me great things; and I had no suspicion at all of any illusion. I saw nothing; but I understood what a great blessing it is to take no account of anything that does not bring us nearer to God. I also understood what it means for a soul to walk in the truth, in the presence of Truth itself.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: Once, when I was reciting the Office with the whole community, my soul suddenly became recollected and seemed to me all bright like a mirror, clear behind, at the sides, above and below; and in its centre I saw Christ our Lord, as I usually see him. It seemed to me that I saw him distinctly in every part of my soul, as in a mirror, and at the same time the mirror was all engraved — I cannot explain it — in our Lord himself, by a most loving communication that I can never describe.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: It seemed to me that this was shown to me like this: as water soaks into a sponge and is drunk up by it, so, it seemed to me, the Divinity filled my soul, which in a certain sense enjoyed and possessed the Three Persons. And I also heard him say: "Do not labour to hold me enclosed within yourself, but enclose yourself within me."
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1904)

items.text: He showed me the book of nature, and I understood that every flower he has created is beautiful, that the brilliance of the rose and the whiteness of the lily do not take away the perfume of the violet or the sweet simplicity of the daisy. I understood that if all the lowly flowers wanted to be roses, nature would lose its springtime beauty, and the fields would no longer be enamelled with lovely colours. And so it is in the world of souls, our Lord's living garden.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: On that blessed night the sweet Infant Jesus, barely an hour old, filled the darkness of my soul with floods of light. By becoming weak and little for love of me, he made me strong and brave; he put his own weapons into my hands, so that I went from victory to victory, beginning, if I may put it so, "to run as a giant." The fountain of my tears dried up, and from then on they flowed neither easily nor often.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: Great good was done in my soul by these beauties of nature, scattered so abundantly everywhere. They lifted it to him who had been pleased to lavish such masterpieces on this passing earth.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: Some time before this I had offered myself to the Child Jesus to be his little plaything. I told him not to treat me like one of those precious toys that children only look at and dare not touch, but like a little ball of no value, which could be thrown on the ground, kicked about, pierced, left in a corner, or pressed to his heart, just as he pleased.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: One evening after Compline I looked in vain for our lamp on the shelves where they are kept, and, as it was the time of the "Great Silence," I could not get it back. … Without the inner light of grace I would undoubtedly have pitied myself, but with that light I felt happy instead of aggrieved, and reflected that poverty means being deprived not only of what is convenient but of what is necessary. And in this outer darkness I found my soul lit by a brightness that was divine.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: Sweet indeed is the way of Love. It is true that we may fall and be unfaithful to grace; but Love, knowing how to draw profit from everything, quickly consumes whatever displeases Jesus, leaving in the heart only a deep and humble peace.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: Our Lord has no need of books or teachers to instruct our souls. He, the Teacher of Teachers, teaches us without any noise of words. I have never heard him speak, yet I know he is within me. He is there, always guiding and inspiring me; and just when I need them, lights I have never seen before break in.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: For me to become great is impossible. I must bear with myself and my many imperfections; but I will look for a way of getting to Heaven by a little way — very short and very straight, a little way that is entirely new. We live in an age of inventions; nowadays the rich need not bother to climb the stairs, they have lifts instead. Well, I mean to try to find a lift to raise me to God, for I am too tiny to climb the steep stairway of perfection.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: He allowed my soul to be overwhelmed with darkness, and the thought of Heaven, which had comforted me from my earliest childhood, now became a source of conflict and torment. This trial has not lasted merely for days or weeks; I have been suffering for months, and I am still waiting for deliverance. I wish I could express what I feel, but it is beyond me. You must have passed through this dark tunnel to understand its blackness.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: As I meditated on these divine words, I saw how imperfect my love for my Sisters in religion was. I understood that I did not love them as our Lord loves them. I know now that true charity consists in bearing with all our neighbours' faults — not being surprised at their weakness, but edified by their smallest virtues.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: For me, prayer is a lifting up of the heart; a glance towards heaven; a cry of gratitude and love, in sorrow and in joy alike. In a word, it is something noble, supernatural, which expands my soul and unites it to God. Sometimes, when I am so spiritually dry that not a single good thought comes to me, I say the "Our Father" or the "Hail Mary" very slowly, and these prayers are enough to take me out of myself and wonderfully refresh me.
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: I understood that love embraces all vocations, that it is all things, and that it reaches out through all the ages and to the farthest ends of the earth, because it is eternal. … O Jesus, my Love, at last I have found my vocation. My vocation is love! Yes, I have found my place in the bosom of the Church, and this place, O my God, you yourself have given me: in the heart of the Church, my Mother, I will be LOVE!
items.author: Thérèse of Lisieux
items.source: The Story of a Soul (modern English, from the translation by Thomas Taylor, 1912)

items.text: Pour yourself out towards it; do not draw its image towards you. … As for the object of contemplation, it matters little. From an Alp to an insect, anything will do, provided your attitude is right: for all the things in this world towards which you reach out are linked together, and one truly grasped will be the gateway to the rest.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: Practical Mysticism (1914, in modern English)

items.text: Because of your new sensitivity, you will hear anthems from every gutter; poems of unbearable loveliness will bud for you on every weed. Best and greatest of all, your fellow men will shine for you with new significance and light. Humility and awe will be stirred in you by the beautiful and patient figures of the poor, their long, silent heroisms, their willing acceptance of the burden of life.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: Practical Mysticism (1914, in modern English)

items.text: Moreover, as your meditation deepens it will defend you from the constant assaults of the outer world. You will hear the busy hum of that world as a distant melody outside you, and know yourself to be in some way withdrawn from it. You have set a ring of silence between you and it; and look! within that silence you are free.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: Practical Mysticism (1914, in modern English)

items.text: Now turn this new, purified and universalised gaze back on yourself. Look at your own being in a fresh relationship with things, and surrender willingly to the moods of astonishment, humility, joy — perhaps of deep shame or sudden love — that invade your heart as you look. Doing this patiently, day after day, constantly recapturing your wandering attention, always renewing the struggle for simplicity of sight, you will at last discover that there is something within you — something behind the fractious, conflicting life of desire — which you can recollect, gather up, and make effective for new life.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: Practical Mysticism (1914, in modern English)

items.text: True contemplation can thrive only when it is protected from two opposite exaggerations: quietism on the one hand, and spiritual fuss on the other. It has nothing to gain from either passivity or anxiety. Though the way may be long and the material of your mind stubborn, ultimate success is assured to the eager lover of Reality.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: Practical Mysticism (1914, in modern English)

items.text: So here is your vocation set out: a vocation so varied in its opportunities that you can hardly fail to find something to do. … You are to work for mercy, order, beauty and significance: to mend where you find things broken, and make where you find the need.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: Practical Mysticism (1914, in modern English)

items.text: And note that this spiritual life we have been considering is not an aristocratic life. Its fundamentals are given by the simplest kinds of traditional piety, and have been shown again and again by the simplest souls. … A little silence and leisure. A great deal of faithfulness, kindness and courage. All this is within reach of anyone who cares enough about it to pay the price.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: The Life of the Spirit and the Life of To-day (1922, in modern English)

items.text: Until we realise that it is better, more useful, more productive of strength, to spend, say, the odd ten minutes in the morning feeling for and finding the Eternal than flicking through the newspaper — that this will send us off to the day's work properly orientated, gathered together, recollected, and truly endowed with new power to deal with circumstances — we have not begun to live the life of the Spirit, or grasped the practical connection between such a daily discipline and the power to do our best work, whatever it may be.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: The Life of the Spirit and the Life of To-day (1922, in modern English)

items.text: Since perfect proof of the supersensual lies beyond the reach of human consciousness, the element of risk can never be removed: in the end we have to trust the universe and live by faith. So the awakened soul must often suffer perplexity and share to the full the stress and anguish of the physical order; and, chained as it is to a consciousness used to responding to that order, must still be content with flashes of understanding and willing to bear long periods of destitution when the light is veiled.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: The Life of the Spirit and the Life of To-day (1922, in modern English)

items.text: As our life matures we discover, to our confusion, that human ears can pick up many incompatible tunes from the Infinite, but cannot hear the whole symphony. And the melody entrusted to us, the one which perhaps only we can contribute and which stretches our powers to the full, holds not only notes of triumph but notes of pain. So the distinctive mark is not happiness but vocation: work demanded and power given, but given only on condition that we spend it, and ourselves, on others without stint.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: The Life of the Spirit and the Life of To-day (1922, in modern English)

items.text: This realisation of ourselves as we truly are — emerging with difficulty from our animal origin, coloured through and through with the self-regarding tendencies and habits it has imprinted on us — this realisation, or self-knowledge, is Humility: the only soil in which the spiritual life can germinate.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: The Life of the Spirit and the Life of To-day (1922, in modern English)

items.text: If the seeking of the Eternal is moved by love, the finding of it comes through prayer. Prayer, in fact — understood as a life or state, not an act or an asking — is the beginning, middle and end of all that we are now considering. … In this world the soul may sometimes wander as if in pastures, and is sometimes poised, breathless and intent. Sometimes it is fed by beauty, sometimes by the most difficult truth, and it experiences the extremes of riches and destitution, darkness and light.
items.author: Evelyn Underhill
items.source: The Life of the Spirit and the Life of To-day (1922, in modern English)

items.text: Love unites the soul with God, and the greater its love, the more deeply it enters into God and the more it is centred in him. In this way of speaking we may say that the centres the soul finds in God are as many as the degrees of its love.
items.author: John of the Cross
items.source: The Living Flame of Love (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 1912)

items.text: This flame of love is the Spirit of the Bridegroom, the Holy Spirit, whose presence within itself the soul is aware of, not only as a fire that consumes it and transforms it in sweet love, but as a fire burning within it, sending out a flame that bathes it in glory and renews it with the refreshment of everlasting life.
items.author: John of the Cross
items.source: The Living Flame of Love (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 1912)

items.text: For when this flame of divine life wounds the soul with a gentle languishing for the life of God, it wounds it with such endearing tenderness, and softens it so much, that it melts away in love.
items.author: John of the Cross
items.source: The Living Flame of Love (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 1912)

items.text: And since the soul cannot act naturally here, or make any efforts of its own except through the bodily senses and with their help — from which in this case it is completely free and most detached — the soul's work is simply to receive what God communicates; for he alone, in the depths of the soul, without the help of the senses, can influence and direct it and work within it.
items.author: John of the Cross
items.source: The Living Flame of Love (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 1912)

items.text: Oh, if only spiritual people knew how much they are losing of the good things of the Spirit, so abundantly provided, because they will not raise their desires above trifles, and how they might have the sweetness of all things in the pure food of the Spirit if only they would give those trifles up.
items.author: John of the Cross
items.source: The Ascent of Mount Carmel (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1864)

items.text: It is a hard and miserable thing for souls when they cannot understand their own state, nor find anyone who can.
items.author: John of the Cross
items.source: The Ascent of Mount Carmel (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, 1864)

items.text: We should bear in mind that a soul, when it is seriously converted to the service of God, is generally nursed and caressed spiritually, like an infant by its loving mother, who warms it at her breast, nourishes it with her own sweet milk, feeds it with tender and delicate food, carries it in her arms and fondles it. But as the child grows, the mother withholds her caresses, hides her breasts and smears them with bitter aloes; she no longer carries the infant in her arms, but makes it walk on the ground, so that, losing the habits of an infant, it may turn to greater and more substantial things.
items.author: John of the Cross
items.source: The Dark Night of the Soul (modern English, from the translation by David Lewis, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 1916)

items.text: I thought of the soul as being like a castle made of a single diamond or of very clear crystal, containing many rooms, just as in heaven there are many mansions.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: If we reflect, sisters, we shall see that the soul of the just is nothing other than a paradise, in which, God tells us, he takes his delight. What, do you imagine, must that dwelling be like in which a King so mighty, so wise and so pure, holding in himself all good, can delight to rest?
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: As far as I can understand, the gate by which to enter this castle is prayer and meditation. I do not mean mental prayer more than vocal prayer, for if it is prayer at all, the mind must take part in it.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: I believe we shall never learn to know ourselves except by trying to know God; for, seeing his greatness, we are struck by our own baseness; his purity shows up our foulness; and by meditating on his humility we find how very far we are from being humble.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: Remember, this is of the greatest importance: the one aim of someone beginning to practise prayer should be to endure trials, and to resolve and strive with all her strength to conform her own will to the will of God.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: I only want to warn you that, to make rapid progress and reach the mansions we wish to enter, what matters is not so much to think much as to love much: so you must do whatever most stirs you to love. Perhaps we do not know what love is, and that does not greatly surprise me. Love does not consist in great sweetness of devotion, but in a fervent determination to try to please God in all things, to avoid as far as possible everything that would offend him, and to pray for the increase of the glory and honour of his Son and for the growth of the Catholic Church.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: I think the surest sign that we keep these two commandments is that we have a genuine love for others. We cannot know whether we love God, although there may be strong reasons for thinking so, but there can be no doubt about whether or not we love our neighbour.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: If you see a sick sister whom you can help, never be afraid of losing your devotion; have compassion on her; if she is in pain, feel it as if it were your own, and when there is need, fast so that she may eat — not so much for her sake as because you know your Lord asks it of you. This is the true union of our will with the will of God.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: Life is long and full of crosses, and we need to look to Christ, our pattern, to see how he bore his trials, and even to follow the example of his Apostles and saints if we want to bear our own trials perfectly. Our good Jesus and his most blessed Mother are too good company to leave, and he is well pleased if we grieve at his pains, even if sometimes at the cost of our own consolations and joys.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: It would be strange to imagine that we could gain these graces by any road other than the one by which Jesus and all his saints have gone before us. Let us not dream of such a thing: believe me, Martha and Mary must both welcome our Lord and keep him as their guest, and they must not be so inhospitable as to offer him no food. How can Mary do this while she sits at his feet, if her sister does not help her?
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: In short, my sisters, I will end with this advice: do not build towers without a foundation, for our Lord does not care so much about how important our works are as about the love with which they are done. When we do all we can, His Majesty will enable us to do more every day.
items.author: Teresa of Ávila
items.source: The Interior Castle (modern English, from the translation by the Benedictines of Stanbrook, rev. Benedict Zimmerman, 3rd ed. 1921)

items.text: Lift up your heart to God with a meek stirring of love; and mean God himself, and none of his good things.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Cloud of Unknowing (ed. Evelyn Underhill, 2nd ed. 1922, in modern English)

items.text: This darkness and this cloud, whatever you do, is between you and your God, and keeps you from either seeing him clearly by the light of understanding in your reason, or feeling him in the sweetness of love in your affection. So prepare yourself to stay in this darkness as long as you can, always crying out after him whom you love.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Cloud of Unknowing (ed. Evelyn Underhill, 2nd ed. 1922, in modern English)

items.text: Look forwards now and let what is behind be; see what you lack, not what you have, for that is the quickest way of gaining and keeping meekness.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Cloud of Unknowing (ed. Evelyn Underhill, 2nd ed. 1922, in modern English)

items.text: For this reason: he may well be loved, but not thought. By love he may be gained and held; but by thought, never.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Cloud of Unknowing (ed. Evelyn Underhill, 2nd ed. 1922, in modern English)

items.text: And strike that thick cloud of unknowing with a sharp dart of longing love; and do not leave it, whatever happens.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Cloud of Unknowing (ed. Evelyn Underhill, 2nd ed. 1922, in modern English)

items.text: And if you would like to have this intent wrapped and folded into one word, so that you can hold on to it better, take just a little word of one syllable: one syllable is better than two, for the shorter it is, the better it suits the work of the Spirit. And such a word is this word GOD, or this word LOVE. Choose whichever you like, or another, as you please — whichever word of one syllable you like best. And fasten this word to your heart, so that it never leaves it, whatever happens.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Cloud of Unknowing (ed. Evelyn Underhill, 2nd ed. 1922, in modern English)

items.text: For virtue is nothing other than an ordered and measured affection, directed plainly to God for his own sake.
items.author: The Cloud of Unknowing
items.source: The Cloud of Unknowing (ed. Evelyn Underhill, 2nd ed. 1922, in modern English)
